chat.said: I need to accelerate securing funding within the next 2 months. We've been focused on investment firms that do deals between £1-2 million, mostly based in the UK. We'll keep sending cold emails and trying to find warm connections, but I want to explore alternatives to support the funding process, as we'll run out of money soon. For example, angel investors might be able to provide a small amount of funding quicker to buy us more time, but we would need to decide whether the overhead would be worth it.

answer.text: An angel bridge could buy time if cash arrives before you run out and its overhead does not undermine the institutional raise. Temporary spend deferral is another possibility, provided it protects delivery and fundability.

why.text: Receiving some funding is not the same as securing enough cash in time.
The bridge comparison includes fees and displaced fundraising effort, but leaves dilution, governance and failed-deal costs unresolved.

text.text: Map cash deadlines against completion steps with prospective investors. Earlier cleared angel cash would support the speed hypothesis; shared diligence delays would challenge it.

chat.said: we have £180,000 cash on hand and spend about £60,000 a month

answer.text: The model now uses your cash of 180,000 GBP and monthly spending of about 60,000 GBP/month, replacing the unspecified cash position. The key distinction is whether spending means net cash burn after incoming revenue. That determines how urgently a bridge is needed, rather than just whether it adds cash.

why.text: Cash is provisionally treated as fully available and spending as net burn. Restricted funds or additional payments could change the deadline.

text.text: Can you confirm whether cash is unrestricted and spending includes incoming revenue and committed payments? This would test whether the model understates your funding urgency.
